title: Fabrication and Characterization of Optical Tissue Phantoms Containing Macrostructure
protocol: Find absorption and reduced scattering coefficients for biological tissue at imaging wavelengths.
Select concentrations of India ink and titanium dioxide (TiO2) to approximate desired optical properties using look-up tables.
Fabricate a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) slab for confirmation of optical properties.
Mix PDMS resin, TiO2, India ink, and PDMS curing agent in a 10:1 weight ratio.
Pour PDMS resin into the mixing cup first.
Add TiO2 to the PDMS resin in the mixing cup.
Add India ink to the mixture in the mixing cup.
Add PDMS curing agent to the mixture in the mixing cup.
Mix in a speed mixer for 60 s.
If TiO2 particles stick to the mixing cup, mix by hand to remove the particles from the base of the cup.
Mix in the mixer for another 30 s.
Pour the mixture into wells or Petri dishes to make thin (0.1-1 mm) slabs of the mixture.
Degas the slabs for 10 min by placing them in an air-tight negative pressure chamber.
Place the degassed slabs in a pre-heated oven at 80 °C for 30-60 min.
Remove from oven and let cool.
Trim off the edges to leave a flat, uniform slab.
Measure the thickness of the slab using calipers.
Measure transmittance (T) and reflectance (R) of slab(s) using an integrating sphere.
Turn on the light source and spectrometer of the integrating sphere setup.
Check the alignment of the system to ensure a small, collimated beam is centered on the entry and exit ports of the integrating sphere.
Cap the exit port of the integrating sphere and record three dark spectra.
Obtain the transmission reference with the exit port capped and the entrance port empty.
Record three spectra.
Obtain reflectance reference measurements using reflectance standard(s).
Place each standard at the exit port of the sphere.
Record three spectra for each reflectance standard.
Measure the transmittance of the slab.
With the cap on the exit port, place the slab on the entry port of the integrating sphere for the transmission measurement.
Record three spectra.
Measure the reflectance of the slab.
Remove the exit port cap and place the slab on the exit port for the reflectance measurement.
Record three spectra.
Determine optical properties using IAD software.
Average the three spectra acquired for each measurement.
Convert these measurements to R and T values using the equations in the IAD manual.
If necessary, condense the files by reducing the sampling rate along the spectrum.
Prepare the input .rxt file with wavelengths, reflectance, transmittance, and sample thickness as described in the IAD manual.
Using the command prompt (Windows OS) or terminal (Mac OS), navigate to the correct path.
Type "iad 'input file name'" to run IAD.
The software will produce an output text file with the estimated optical properties.
Design internal structure using computer aided design (CAD) software.
Convert the solid model to a stereolithography file for fabrication on a 3D printer.
If available, convert a segmented CT scan into a stereolithography file.
Select a dissolvable material for printing, such as poly-vinyl alcohol or high-impact polystyrene.
Print the solid model in the selected dissolvable material.
Break, dissolve, or machine off the support material from the printed part when cooled sufficiently.
File or sand off any large imperfections on the printed part.
Vapor polish the printed part to reduce surface roughness.
Secure the printed part in a vice and drill a through hole for a thin steel or nitinol wire.
Thread a stainless steel or nitinol wire through the drilled hole.
Bend the ends of the wire and hook them together.
Fill a large beaker roughly 10% full with acetone.
Place the beaker on a hot plate while heating to 100 °C.
Set up the printed part with attached wire for full immersion in acetone vapor within the beaker.
When acetone vapor condensation reaches about halfway up the wall of the beaker, hang the looped wire with the mock airway on a second wire and suspend in acetone vapor for 15-30 s.
Ensure printed parts do not touch the beaker walls or each other during vapor polishing.
Remove printed part and suspend over empty beaker or container.
Let part dry for at least 4 h.
Verify the dimensions of the internal structure are within tolerance to the CAD design as needed.
Design a solid model base of the mold to 3D print.
Print a base for the mold with an inset to secure the sidings.
Place sidings in the recesses of the mold base.
Seal the edges of the mold with heat resistant tape.
Place a polycarbonate base plate inside the mold.
Glue the fully-dried vapor polished part to the base plate.
Allow sufficient time for glue to dry.
Pour 9.1 g of PDMS resin into a plastic mixing cup.
Add 20 mg of rutile TiO2 to the PDMS resin.
Add 35 µl of India ink to the mixture.
Add 0.91 g of curing agent to the top of the mixture.
Pour final polymer mixture into the heat-resistant mold.
Pour a small amount of the mixture into a separate container to create a polymer slab for confirmation of material optical properties.
Ensure enough polymer is poured to have a slab of at least 100 µm thickness.
Place both the mock airway mold and the separate slab into a bell jar for degassing.
Begin vacuum process.
If the polymer in the mock airway mold starts to rise, let the air back into the bell jar to burst the surface bubbles, then begin to pull air again.
Repeat this process until the polymer no longer rises significantly.
Continue to degas for another 15 min after the polymer stops rising significantly.
Slowly let the air back into the chamber.
Remove both the mock airway phantom and the polymer slab from the bell jar.
Place them in a level oven at 80 °C for 2 h.
After 2 hours, remove the phantom and slab from the oven and let cool for 20 min.
Disassemble the polymer mold with a scalpel without cutting the cured polymer.
Snap the base plate off of the mock-airway base.
Place the phantom in a heated (60 °C) ~0.5 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH) base bath until the internal part is fully dissolved.
Once the internal structure is dissolved, take the phantom out of the bath and let it fully dry (~24 h) before taking any optical measurements.
Verify phantom geometry using high resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or micro-computed tomography (CT) imaging.
Alternatively, verify optical properties of the phantom using an optically clear reference phantom and integrating sphere.
Image the phantom with 20 µm resolution in all dimensions if using micro-CT.
